judgments.identification: JavaScript Plex timeline-SSRF and transcoder codec-write exploit implementation
evidence: Module-level code uses a fresh client ID and junk X-Plex-Token, starts proxy polling, then sends timeline subscribe/unsubscribe requests. The protocol value is a loopback Plex agent-search URL; its identifier is the plugin network-fetch function with an off-host loopback-prefix DNS name. This is an active request sender, rather than a renderer of request material.

The caller-supplied owner token is installed in headers. A PUT sets TranscoderH264Options to dump video data into a .so in the Codecs set directory; an external caller-selected carrier is transcoded, the option is cleared, and transcoding is repeated. The staged library and native loader are not embedded in this script.

The fixed receiver has a reserved .test suffix, and the codec set directory is a placeholder. These limit effectiveness but do not remove the deliberately implemented exploit requests. No successful token leak, library write or payload execution is claimed.

judgments.identification: code-zm plex2shell, exact upstream Python operator-side exploit CLI
evidence: The SHA-256 of the script recovered with forager from the upstream repository matches the supplied sample exactly. It is publicly disclosed GPL security-testing code, not an established trojanized library. That provenance is a legitimate-use consideration, not a scanner corroboration or proof of authorization.

main requires a target and callback address, starts a TCP listener, and by default calls steal_owner_token. That routine uses a concurrent proxy poll and timeline subscribe/unsubscribe requests to drive a loopback agent-search request, a plugin GetResultFromNetwork target, and a loopback-prefix sslip.io receiver. TokenCatcher collects the X-Plex-Token header and accepts a local-* token. --token instead bypasses this capture stage.

The owner token is used for preferences and resource reads. The transcoder resource response is searched for the codec set ID. Platform settings select Linux/native, Linux/container, or Windows codec roots. Windows LocalAppDataPath is parsed from preferences where available.

The payload builders read sibling C templates, substitute caller-selected callback information, and invoke GCC or MinGW with shared-library arguments. Those C templates are absent from the supplied standalone file; matching upstream sources were recovered as context in scratch. They are not asserted to be embedded payloads.

build_carrier puts native payload bytes at the start of frame-zero luma, pads the luma and chroma planes with 0x80, writes three raw frames, and invokes ffmpeg with libx264 qp=0 plus silent audio. It decodes the resulting file and checks the reconstructed prefix against the original payload bytes. The HTTP listener serves media XML and the carrier, including Range responses.

The computed codec path is inserted in dump-yuv=%s:qp=0 and submitted via an owner-authenticated preferences PUT. A first transcode is intended to write payload bytes there; clearing the option and transcoding again is intended to trigger codec loading. The rule now binds the constructed path to that dump operand; it does not infer a library suffix from the variable name.

The Linux shell command binds stdin to an outbound /dev/tcp connection, aliases stdout/stderr to that descriptor, then runs script -qc /bin/bash for an interactive terminal. The recovered Linux library constructor forks and execs /bin/sh -c with this command. The recovered Windows DLL starts a rundll32 child; its exported routine connects back, receives commands and returns cmd.exe output. These upstream templates corroborate the intended build path but cannot prove a deployed library exists.

The operator can run one supplied command or use an interactive session. The Linux session removes the codec file and configures terminal I/O; preferences are reset in finally. No root escalation, boot persistence, or covert attack against the operator machine was established.

The explicit testing banner, caller-configured target, and public source make authorized assessment plausible. The chosen verdict follows the victim-machine assessment requested here: its primary default operation obtains an owner token through an access-control exploit and turns it into a remote shell. Public distribution and an authorization banner do not establish that a found operational copy is authorized.

judgments.identification: PowerShell Plex timeline-SSRF and transcoder codec-write exploit implementation
evidence: The script accepts a base endpoint, owner token, and carrier URL. Start-Job sends a junk-token proxy poll; the main run sends timeline subscribe/unsubscribe requests with a full loopback HTTP URL in protocol and the nested plugin network-fetch identifier. The fixed callback host has a reserved .test suffix.

It then uses the supplied OwnerToken for preferences PUTs. Its dump-yuv output names a DLL inside a Windows Plex Codecs set directory. It transcodes the supplied carrier, resets the preference, and transcodes again. This sends the exploitation requests; it neither contains the carrier library nor captures an owner token automatically.

Caller-supplied token/media, placeholder codec set and reserved callback prevent a claim of observed success. The hardcoded injection target and two-pass transcode sequence nevertheless establish a deliberate exploit attempt, rather than ordinary media conversion.

shared_limits: All three supplied artifacts are plain scripts with no archive members or embedded decoded payload layers. All supplied hashes were verified. Their obfuscation is URL percent-encoding of nested request values; no encrypted or packed program was found.

No exploit traffic, compiler, shell, or native payload was executed. trace.py compiles only five inspected function ASTs with a recording HTTP transport and fake token catcher; its output confirms the nested request construction without testing a Plex server. JavaScript and PowerShell were traced directly from complete source; their native runtimes were unavailable.

No host ownership, engagement authorization, server version, final carrier bytes, successful callback, or final service-account authority was supplied. The verdicts concern active exploit artifacts, not a proven infection, malware family, or covert registry compromise.
The upstream README and C templates are first-party source context. No feed, scanner report, advisory conviction, or repository name was used to establish malicious behavior.

trait_repairs.placement_only: 17 observations/aggregates move to their supported subjects; check.py verifies identical effective matchers, exclusions, scopes, criticality and confidence against HEAD. The matchers were retained rather than suppressed for this batch.
unsupported_claims: gcc/clang string literals and their aggregate do not prove a compiler process was launched or compilation happened after delivery. They move to source-name metadata, and unsupported T1027.004 mappings are removed.
httpd matched a Python attribute assignment. Preserve the name reference in metadata, rather than labeling it daemon activity.
A shell export assignment is not an HTTP download or a file writer. Preserve command-text evidence under environment writes and update its exact download-profile exclusion.

An open(...).write(...) text pattern observes call syntax, which can occur in quoted code; move it to source call syntax. Retain the independent parsed chained-write capability and describe that as a call rather than guaranteed file creation.
Codecs paths describe a library location rather than generic application data. Preserve the matcher and add the exact moved trait to three former app-data directory consumers.

host/key/secret/user/password/DSN vocabulary alone does not prove database configuration or secret acquisition. Preserve the field observations and their exact aggregate under source key-value metadata; the database-collection consumer retains the same key evidence alongside its existing read/path conditions.
SSRF/LFI attack-class words and their aggregate describe names, not data parsing. Preserve them under source naming metadata and retain the exact labeled-corpus exception member set.

narrowing.unsupported_claim: An arbitrary helper return mentioning lhost/lport was previously labeled a shell template. Require a returned string expression with actual shell-path/TCP-command text, including f/raw strings. The sample now matches its real revshell_cmd return, not build_payload_windows dispatch. Existing Bash/PTY attack fixtures remain matched.

additions: A suspicious AST rule binds a formatted Codecs-directory path through its joined destination into the TranscoderH264Options dump-yuv operand, including capture by an inner function. Unrelated destination, other directory and other option controls do not match.

A hostile reverse-shell composite requires a returned shell string and the TCP stdin/stdout/stderr shell-command structure in the same expression. A suspicious atom describes the command text; neither claims that the generator machine connects.
PowerShell Uri.EscapeDataString call syntax now receives notable URL-encoding coverage.
Custom X-token header matching admits PowerShell equals syntax as well as colon fields; it rejects equality comparisons and preserves the existing JavaScript positive.
trait_repairs.ancestor_consumers: Exact references follow moves. Three fs/path/app-data selectors retain the exact Codecs path member and the data/manipulation exclusion retains the exact moved open-write text member. Compiler-name-only strings intentionally cease to satisfy generic process/create/shell selectors; they cannot establish execution. The shell-only carried-source compiler consumer cannot see the moved Python-only literals. The HTTP-download selector intentionally no longer accepts a bare export assignment. Actual subprocess/HTTP/write attack observations are retained.
